see: A second leaf blower starts but it doesn't sound twice as loud
is: Two equal sources add only 3 dB; it takes about 10 dB to sound twice as loud

see: My meter shows different numbers in dBA and dBC
is: They are different filters; dBC keeps the bass that dBA turns down

see: A report lists Leq, Lmax and L90 and I don't know which matters
is: Leq is the average, Lmax the loudest moment, L90 the background

see: The airport says my street is DNL 60
is: A 24-hour year average with a 10 dB night penalty; the FAA's standard metric

see: A European noise map shows Lden and Lnight
is: EU 24-hour and night averages with evening and night penalties
anchor: What are DNL and Lden?

see: Highway hum that carries for blocks
is: Roads act as line sources and lose only about 3 dB per doubling of distance

see: A jackhammer that fades quickly as I walk away
is: A point source loses about 6 dB each time you double the distance

see: Tall concrete walls along the highway
is: Noise barriers cut about 5-10 dB(A), up to about 20 dB(A)
anchor: Do noise barriers work?

see: Neighbor's bass thumps through the wall but no words
is: Walls block low frequencies far less, and bass travels through structure

see: Sirens echo between tall buildings downtown
is: Hard parallel surfaces reflect sound back and add to the level

see: Is my phone's decibel app right?
is: Good iOS apps come within about 2 dBA; Android varies by device

see: How loud is a whisper compared with a jet?
is: About 30 dB versus about 120 dB on the audiology chart
anchor: How loud is loud? A rough decibel ruler

see: Do I have to shout to be heard here?
is: Shouting at 3 ft means likely 95 dBA or more, per NIOSH
anchor: How loud is loud? A rough decibel ruler

see: Where can I find a noise map for my street?
is: BTS publishes a modeled US national map; the EU requires maps by law

see: Ringing in my ears after a concert
is: Tinnitus; NIDCD says noise-caused tinnitus may fade or, in some cases, last for life.

see: I have to shout to be heard at work
is: Likely 95 dBA or more, per NIOSH's arm's-length rule of thumb.
anchor: How loud is too loud for your ears?

see: Is my lawn mower or power tool loud enough to hurt my hearing
is: NIOSH puts these around 85-90 dBA, at or above its 8-hour limit.
anchor: How loud is too loud for your ears?

see: Headphones turned up all the way
is: Can reach 94-110 dBA per NIDCD; at 100 dBA NIOSH recommends no more than 15 minutes a day.
anchor: How long can I listen at 100 decibels?

see: A loud club or concert all night
is: Bars and clubs are often 95 dBA or more; WHO's venue standard caps 100 dB LAeq over 15 minutes.
anchor: How long can I listen at 100 decibels?

see: Hearing seems fine but tests show a dip
is: An audiometric notch; CDC found one in 23.5% of adults who rated their hearing excellent or good.
anchor: How many people already have noise damage?

see: Traffic outside all night keeping me up
is: WHO 2018 recommends road noise below 45 dB Lnight outside the home.
anchor: What are the WHO noise guidelines?

see: Planes overhead at night
is: WHO 2018 sets aircraft at below 40 dB Lnight and 45 dB Lden, its strictest values.
anchor: What are the WHO noise guidelines?

see: Noise wakes me up even when it is not that loud
is: WHO 2009 reported 42 dB Lnight outside as a threshold for waking.
anchor: What decibel level is safe for sleeping?

see: A restaurant getting louder as it fills up
is: The Lombard effect: people automatically raise their voices in noise.
anchor: Why do restaurants get so loud?

see: Living next to a busy road for years
is: WHO's 2018 review linked road noise to about 8% higher heart disease risk per 10 dB Lden.
anchor: Can traffic noise cause heart disease?

see: School under a flight path
is: RANCH linked aircraft noise at schools to slower reading in children.
anchor: Do airplanes affect children's learning?

see: Chewing sounds make me furious
is: Misophonia: decreased tolerance to specific sounds, per a 2022 consensus definition.
anchor: What is misophonia vs hyperacusis?

see: Everyday sounds feel painfully loud
is: Hyperacusis: a disproportionate increase in perceived loudness of normal-volume sounds (ICD-10 H93.23).

see: My phone warned me about my weekly listening
is: WHO-ITU H.870 devices track a weekly sound allowance, 80 dB for 40 hours for adults.

see: Earplugs that say NRR 33
is: Real protection is usually lower; OSHA and NIOSH derate the label.

is: Some codes, like New York City's and Toronto's, set dBC or octave-band limits aimed at bass.

is: NYC caps commercial music at 42 dB(A) inside your home.
